name: Status Quo Bias
statement: People disproportionately prefer keeping their current state of affairs over switching to an alternative, even a better one.
statementAccent: disproportionately prefer keeping their current state of affairs over switching to an alternative
meaning: Status quo bias is the tendency to favour the existing option or default simply because it is the current one, treating any deviation as a potential loss even when the alternative may be objectively superior. It was documented as a systematic decision pattern distinct from, though related to, general loss aversion. It appears across personal choices, organisational decisions, and public policy defaults.
mechanism: The bias arises from several overlapping mechanisms: loss aversion (losses from switching loom larger than equivalent gains), the endowment effect and mere-exposure familiarity, psychological commitment or sunk-cost thinking, the cognitive effort of evaluating alternatives, and regret avoidance (regret over a bad outcome from action feels worse than from inaction). Together they make keeping the current option the path of least psychological resistance.

examples.text: In their 1988 study, Samuelson and Zeckhauser ran choice experiments in which the same option, when designated the "status quo," was chosen far more often than when presented as one of several neutral alternatives.

Their analysis of real employee choices among health plans and retirement programmes found individuals stuck with previously chosen options at rates far higher than a fully-informed reconsideration would predict.

Comparisons of default auto-insurance rules in New Jersey and Pennsylvania showed that differing default options produced dramatically different final enrolment patterns among otherwise similar drivers.

whyItMatters: Status quo bias is central to behavioural economics and to "nudge" policy design (opt-out retirement savings, organ-donation defaults) because setting the default choice can predictably shape large-scale outcomes without restricting anyone’s options.
limits: Sticking with the status quo is not always irrational. It can reflect real switching costs, uncertainty about alternatives, or genuine information gaps rather than a pure bias. Scholars such as Gal and Rucker argue status quo bias and loss aversion are distinct, since preference for the status quo persists even without a gain/loss frame, suggesting inertia operates as an independent factor.
misreadings: It is sometimes reduced to simple "laziness" or treated as identical to loss aversion, when the documented effect includes cases with no gain/loss framing and other mechanisms like regret avoidance or commitment.
origin: Identified and named by economists William Samuelson and Richard Zeckhauser in their 1988 paper "Status Quo Bias in Decision Making," Journal of Risk and Uncertainty.
